## TL;DR

Stories cards now let story titles, summaries, and live task names wrap on phone widths instead of hiding identifying words behind ellipses. The mobile rules apply at the existing 720px breakpoint, leaving the desktop presentation intact. Task rows have a 44px minimum height for easier tapping, while story progress and status chips remain present. The UI rebuild and requested `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check` passed.

## Work and rationale

The issue was caused by compact desktop-oriented CSS carried into the phone layout. Story names used `white-space: nowrap`, hidden overflow, and ellipsis. The excerpt was limited to two lines. Live task names had the same single-line clipping behavior, despite showing the task identifier and status cue in the same row. The task list therefore provided little value when names were long.

I kept the change inside the existing `@media (max-width: 720px)` block. At that size, story names can wrap and break at long unspaced text, summaries display without the two-line clamp, and task names wrap alongside their existing status cues. The task dot and cue align with the first line, which keeps each row’s visual status readable as the title continues below. A 44px minimum row height and added vertical padding improve touch comfort without changing desktop hit areas.

The progress display retains its existing mobile treatment: it moves to a full-width row beneath the story heading. Status chips remain visible beneath the header and still wrap naturally. No new disclosure control is needed because content is now available inline; the existing story and task buttons still provide access to their detail panels.

I added a source-level regression assertion in the Stories view suite for the key mobile behaviors: wrapping story names and task names, unclamping the excerpt, and maintaining the task row minimum height. This follows the existing test style in that suite, which checks the view’s breakpoint CSS contracts.

The review shot is declared for `/stories`, highlighting a live task title so that the intended content region is visible in the managed capture. The actual seeded capture is performed by RepoOS during handoff.

## Approaches tried

I chose responsive wrapping over a show-more affordance. An expand control would add another interaction to every compact story card and could still leave the first view ambiguous. Allowing text to flow uses the existing card structure and makes more of the story immediately identifiable. I also kept the breakpoint and progress layout unchanged to limit the risk of shifting desktop cards or status information.

I did not add CSS changes to the shared stylesheet because all relevant story-card styles are scoped to `StoriesView.vue`. Keeping the phone-specific rules beside the existing breakpoint makes the interaction between wrapping, progress positioning, and the chevron easier to maintain.

## Challenges and blockers

There were no implementation blockers. The initial RepoOS metadata update printed its standard warning that the linked-worktree CLI reads the canonical board in the main checkout. This is the CLI’s task metadata path; source reads and edits for this task remained in the assigned worktree.

The requested scoped check ran remotely, then completed its local guard steps. The remote run built the app and ran 10 changed-path plus always-run test files, including the Stories view tests; the run passed. Local formatting, lint, build, CSS layer, theme contrast, hard-coded color, rendered contrast, bare-require, artifact, and UI smoke checks passed. The staleness step correctly skipped because this checkout had no RepoOS build marker at that point. Generated `dist/` output remains local and is not part of the task changes.

No physical-device inspection was performed. The behavior was verified through CSS regression assertions, the production UI build, and the repository’s UI smoke test; the managed review shot will provide a visual review capture.

## Key learnings

For narrow story cards, preserving the full task title gives more immediate value than shaving card height. Wrapping must be applied consistently to both the heading and the nested live-task rows; fixing only one still leaves the work ambiguous. Long descriptions need their own mobile override because a line clamp can conceal the distinguishing phrase even when the title is readable. Keeping these changes at the phone breakpoint preserves existing desktop density and leaves progress and status information in their established scan order.
